scenarios.prompt: Both arms stop short overhead; passive range is higher and painless; long-standing.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Ask whether it is new or painful. If long-standing and painless with no warning sign: train in the controlled range, change one thing, re-check in a later session.

scenarios.prompt: The right arm has lost range over recent weeks with no known reason; the client cannot lift it as high themselves.
scenarios.goodAnswer: New unexplained loss of active movement: stop shoulder work; urgent GP or NHS 111 today.

scenarios.prompt: Stiffness for months with pain at night, slowly getting worse.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Do not progress shoulder loading; routine referral now (getting worse).

lesson.title: Mobility and stability: common restrictions
lesson.summary: A missing range is a question to look into, not a label. Learn to tell range from control, what research says about posture, and when a restriction needs referral instead of training.
objectives: Tell active range from passive range, and range from control.
Recognise the restrictions trainers often see: overhead reach, reaching behind the back, reaching across the body.
State what a systematic review found about upper-back posture and shoulder pain, and what it did not show.
Decide when a restriction is a training question and when it needs referral.

blocks.content: A client cannot get the bar overhead, or one hand stops short behind the back. Before you reach for a stretch, ask two questions: how far does the shoulder go, and how well does the client control it there? And before either: is this new?

Mobility is the range a client can reach. Stability, in coaching terms, is how well they control that range, especially under load. They are not opposites; a good session works on both, and the answer to one changes what you do about the other.

Active range is how far the client moves the arm on their own. Passive range is how far it goes when someone else moves it, with the client relaxed. A difference between them is a reason to look closer. It is not a prescription, and this lesson draws no training rule from it.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: A new or substantial loss of active movement with no clear explanation, where the client cannot lift or move the arm themselves even though you could move it for them, is an urgent referral: an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 today. It is never something to train. After a fall or impact, an arm they cannot move is an emergency.

blocks.content: A systematic review found moderate evidence of no significant difference in how rounded the upper back is (thoracic kyphosis) between people with and without shoulder pain. A result that is not significant does not prove the two groups are the same, and the studies varied in quality. The finding is about association; it does not show that posture causes or prevents shoulder pain.

In single-session studies, people reached more maximum shoulder range when sitting or standing upright than when slouched, with or without shoulder pain. Whether that matters over weeks of training is not known.

content.label: Coach note
content.text: Avoid telling clients that their posture is damaging their shoulder; the research above does not show that. You can still use an upright set-up when it helps a lift, as a coaching choice.

content: Overhead reach: the arms stop short of vertical, or the lower back arches to get there.
Reaching behind the back: one hand stops lower on the spine than the other.
Reaching across the body: one elbow stops further from the opposite shoulder.
Ask first: is this new, and does it hurt? If it is new, unexplained or painful, go to the stop-and-refer rules before any screen.
Wall reach: the client stands with their back against a wall, then raises both arms forward and up as far as is comfortable. Note where the hands stop and whether the lower back leaves the wall.
Lying reach: the client lies on their back with knees bent and raises both arms overhead toward the floor behind them. Compare sides.

Active then passive, only with permission: after the client raises the arm on their own, support it at the elbow and wrist and see whether it goes further without pain. Never push; stop at the first discomfort.
Write down what you saw in plain words, for example: "right hand stops about a hand's width short of the wall overhead."

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Stop the screen, and stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session, if pain comes on or rises. Pain that is getting worse over the following days: routine referral now. Stiffness or pain that has not improved after 2 weeks, or pain at night with stiffness that does not go away: routine referral. A new inability to lift the arm themselves: urgent, today. Pins and needles that do not go away: urgent, today. This screen never clears anyone and never names an injury.

blocks.content: For a long-standing, familiar restriction that does not hurt and shows no warning sign: train in the range the client controls, change one thing at a time, and re-check in a later session. Anything new, unexplained or painful goes to the stop-and-refer rules first.

Some coaching systems explain restrictions with fascial lines or rib position. They can be useful ways to talk about movement with a client. Spindle does not teach them as explanations of how the body works.

content.prompt: A systematic review compared upper-back rounding (thoracic kyphosis) in people with and without shoulder pain. What did it find?
options: People with shoulder pain had much more rounded upper backs
No significant difference between the groups, with moderate evidence; that does not prove the groups are the same
content.explanation: The review found moderate evidence of no significant difference in thoracic kyphosis between people with and without shoulder pain. That does not prove the groups are the same, and it does not show cause either way.

content.prompt: In single-session studies, how did upright posture compare with slouching for maximum shoulder range?
options: More range when upright; whether it matters over time is not known
content.explanation: People reached more maximum range upright than slouched in single sessions; the long-term relevance is unclear.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: A client cannot reach fully overhead on either side. With permission you can lift both arms higher, and nothing hurts. What do you ask before you plan anything? Now change one thing: the right arm has lost range over the last few weeks for no reason the client knows of. What changes?
